meta.title: Who really said "Everyone sees what you appear to be, few experience what you really are"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it’s genuinely Machiavelli, from The Prince (1532), chapter 18. The Italian “pochi sentono quello che tu se’” is loosely rendered “few experience what you really are.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everyone sees what you appear to be, few experience what you really are'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Machiavelli — The Prince (1532), ch. 18. A looser English rendering of “pochi sentono quello che tu se’” (‘few feel what you are’).

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1469–1527 · Florentine diplomat & political theorist; written 1513, published 1532
answer.sourceLine: From ‘The Prince’ (Il Principe), chapter 18, “Concerning the Way in Which Princes Should Keep Faith.” The line translates Machiavelli’s “Ognuno vede quello che tu pari, pochi sentono quello che tu se’” — the popular English swaps ‘feel/know’ for ‘experience.’

source.heading: The Prince, chapter 18

docMeta.dd: 18 — “Concerning the Way in Which Princes Should Keep Faith”

source.excerpt: For that reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest… and men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand… Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them.
trail: The English sentence “Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are…” appears in chapter 18 of the standard translation of The Prince ↗.
The Italian original — “Ognuno vede quello che tu pari, pochi sentono quello che tu se’” — is credited to Machiavelli’s Il Principe ↗.
The line sits inside Machiavelli’s argument that a ruler is judged by appearances because “men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand,” per the Lit2Go text ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner lifts the middle clause
source.excerptNote: Original Italian: “Ognuno vede quello che tu pari, pochi sentono quello che tu se’.” The verb ‘sentono’ means ‘feel/perceive’; the widely shared “few experience what you really are” is a looser modern rendering of the same sentence, while the classic W. K. Marriott translation reads “few really know what you are.”
source.rightsNote: The Prince (1532) and its pre-1929 English translations are in the public domain.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: About Niccolò Machiavelli
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political philosopher whose 1513 treatise The Prince — written after the Medici returned to power and cost him his republican post — became the founding text of modern political realism. Chapter 18 is his most notorious: it argues a ruler must know how to be both ‘the fox and the lion,’ and that in politics appearance routinely outweighs reality.

context.heading: Appearance over reality
lead: Chapter 18 is Machiavelli’s defense of the ruler who lies well. Because a prince cannot always keep faith and survive, he must be a skilled ‘dissembler’ — and he can get away with it because the public only ever sees the surface. “Men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand,” Machiavelli writes: everyone sees what you appear to be, and the few who perceive what you truly are are outnumbered and outgunned by the majesty of the state.
detailsBody: The line is often quoted as timeless wisdom about authenticity, but in its original setting it is coldly instrumental: it explains why cultivating a false but pleasing image is a workable strategy for holding power. That gap — between the self-help reading and Machiavelli’s realpolitik — is part of why the sentence travels so well.
context.pull: Men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand.
